_meta.notes: Comprehensive index for Saint Vincent and the Grenadines covering Ciboney/Arawak/Kalinago indigenous peoples, fierce Kalinago resistance (British struggled to colonize), Black Caribs/Garifuna formation (escaped African slaves + Kalinago), First/Second Carib Wars (1769-73, 1795-97), Garifuna deportation to Honduras 1797, French-British rivalry, sugar/slavery economy, emancipation 1834, independence 1979, La Soufrière volcano eruptions (1902 killed 1,600; 1979 evacuation; 2021 eruption), and multi-island nation.

religion.note: Protestant dominant (Anglican established church, Methodist/Seventh-day Adventist/Pentecostal); small Catholic; Rastafari visible (cultural influence exceeds numbers); syncretic African-Christian practices

ethnic_groups.name: Black/African descent
ethnic_groups.notes: Descendants of enslaved Africans; Afro-Caribbean identity; Garifuna heritage (Black Caribs deported 1797 but legacy remains)

ethnic_groups.name: Indigenous
ethnic_groups.notes: Kalinago/Garifuna heritage (most deported 1797); near extinction but cultural survival

country_profile.notes_unique: Last Caribbean island to be colonized by Europeans (fierce Kalinago resistance); Black Caribs/Garifuna people (escaped African slaves + Kalinago, unique ethnogenesis); Garifuna Wars (1795-97, led by Joseph Chatoyer national hero); 5,000 Garifuna deported to Honduras 1797 (Sebarú deportation, April 12 Garifuna Settlement Day); La Soufrière volcano (active, eruptions 1718/1812/1902 killed 1,600/1979 evacuation/2021 major eruption); Pirates of the Caribbean filming location (Bequia/Grenadines); 32 islands/cays (Grenadines shared with Grenada); Mustique (celebrity playground); yachting/sailing destination

910.name: Indigenous Peoples of Hairouna
910.description: The pre-Columbian indigenous civilizations of Saint Vincent (known to the Caribs as Hairouna, 'land of the blessed') and the Grenadine islands, from early Ciboney peoples through the Arawak and Kalinago (Island Carib) communities that fiercely defended the islands for centuries after European contact.

sub_clusters.name: Ciboney and Arawak Settlement
sub_clusters.description: The earliest inhabitants, the Ciboney, settled Saint Vincent around 5000 BCE, followed by Arawak peoples who migrated from South America's Orinoco region. They established agricultural and fishing communities across the main island and several Grenadine islands.

sub_clusters.name: Kalinago (Carib) Dominance
sub_clusters.description: The Kalinago (Island Caribs) conquered and displaced the Arawak, establishing warrior communities and naming Saint Vincent 'Hairouna.' Their fierce resistance to European colonization made Saint Vincent one of the last Caribbean islands to be colonized, remaining under indigenous control until the 18th century.
key_events: Kalinago establish control over Saint Vincent and resist European incursion for over 250 years after Columbus

920.name: European Contact and Carib Resistance
920.description: Columbus's sighting of Saint Vincent in 1498, the arrival of shipwrecked and escaped enslaved Africans who intermarried with the Kalinago to form the Black Caribs (Garifuna), and the sustained indigenous resistance that kept European colonizers at bay for over two centuries.

sub_clusters.name: Columbus Sighting and Early European Contact
sub_clusters.description: Columbus sighted Saint Vincent on January 22, 1498 (Saint Vincent's Day). However, the fierce Kalinago resistance prevented any European settlement. The island was declared a neutral Carib territory by agreement between France and Britain in 1660.

sub_clusters.name: Emergence of the Garifuna (Black Caribs)
sub_clusters.description: Shipwrecked enslaved Africans from passing slave ships (notably from a wreck around 1635) and escaped enslaved people from neighboring islands intermarried with the Kalinago, creating a distinct Afro-indigenous people known as the Black Caribs (Garifuna). They became the dominant group on Saint Vincent and developed their own language and culture.
key_events: African survivors from shipwrecked slave vessels integrate with Kalinago c. 1635
Garifuna (Black Caribs) become the predominant population on Saint Vincent

930.name: Colonial Wars and the Carib Wars
930.description: The intensifying Anglo-French rivalry over Saint Vincent, the development of sugar plantations, and the dramatic Carib Wars in which the Garifuna under Paramount Chief Joseph Chatoyer fought to defend their homeland — ending in defeat and mass deportation.

sub_clusters.name: French Settlement and Sugar Plantations
sub_clusters.description: French settlers gradually encroached on Saint Vincent from neighboring Martinique, establishing sugar plantations in the Leeward valleys while the Windward side remained under Carib control. The Treaty of Paris (1763) ceded Saint Vincent to Britain.

sub_clusters.name: The First Carib War
sub_clusters.description: British attempts to survey and distribute Carib lands provoked the First Carib War (1769–1773). The Caribs, led by Chief Joseph Chatoyer, fought effectively and secured a treaty that recognized a Carib territory on the Windward side of the island.
key_events: First Carib War 1769–1773 — Caribs secure territorial treaty

sub_clusters.name: The Second Carib War and Garifuna Deportation
sub_clusters.description: Inspired by the French Revolution, the Garifuna under Paramount Chief Joseph Chatoyer allied with the French and launched the Second Carib War in 1795. Chatoyer was killed in battle on March 14, 1795. After British victory, approximately 5,000 Garifuna were rounded up and deported to Roatán Island off Honduras in 1797 — one of the Caribbean's most tragic forced removals.
key_events: Paramount Chief Joseph Chatoyer killed in battle — March 14, 1795 (now National Heroes Day)
British deport approximately 5,000 Garifuna to Roatán — 1797

940.name: Emancipation and 19th-Century Transformations
940.description: The post-Carib War expansion of the plantation system, emancipation in 1834, the importation of indentured laborers, devastating La Soufrière eruptions, and the social and economic transitions of the post-slavery era.

sub_clusters.name: Expanded Plantations and Emancipation
sub_clusters.description: After the Garifuna deportation, British planters expanded sugar estates across the entire island. Emancipation came in 1834 with an apprenticeship period ending in 1838. Portuguese, East Indian, and other indentured laborers were subsequently imported to supplement the labor force.

sub_clusters.name: La Soufrière Eruptions and Post-Emancipation Society
sub_clusters.description: La Soufrière volcano erupted violently in 1812, devastating the northern part of the island and killing dozens. In the post-emancipation period, freed people established smallholder agriculture, growing arrowroot (Saint Vincent became the world's largest producer) alongside provisions. The planter class declined as sugar became less profitable.
key_events: La Soufrière eruption of 1812 — major destruction in northern Saint Vincent

950.name: 20th Century: Eruptions, Labour Movement, and Independence
950.description: The catastrophic 1902 La Soufrière eruption, the rise of the labour movement, banana economy development, and the path to independence in 1979 under Milton Cato.

sub_clusters.name: 1902 La Soufrière Eruption and Early 20th Century
sub_clusters.description: La Soufrière erupted catastrophically on May 7–8, 1902 (the same week as Mount Pelée in Martinique), killing approximately 1,600 people — mostly Carib descendants in the northern part of the island. The eruption devastated agriculture and deepened poverty.
key_events: La Soufrière eruption — May 7, 1902 — approximately 1,600 killed

sub_clusters.name: Labour Movement and Banana Economy
sub_clusters.description: The labour movement grew through the 1930s and 1940s, with Ebenezer Theodore Joshua and later Robert Milton Cato emerging as key political figures. Bananas became the dominant export crop under Commonwealth preferential trade agreements, transforming the agricultural landscape. Universal suffrage was achieved in 1951.

sub_clusters.name: Independence — October 27, 1979
sub_clusters.description: Saint Vincent gained associated statehood in 1969 and achieved full independence on October 27, 1979, under Prime Minister Milton Cato. La Soufrière erupted again on April 13, 1979, just months before independence, forcing the evacuation of 20,000 people but causing no deaths — a stark contrast to 1902.
key_events: La Soufrière eruption — April 13, 1979 — 20,000 evacuated, no deaths
Independence of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines — October 27, 1979

960.name: Contemporary Saint Vincent and the Grenadines
960.description: Post-independence challenges and developments: banana trade disputes, Grenadines tourism (especially Mustique), the 2021 La Soufrière eruption, climate vulnerability, and the legacy of Garifuna heritage.

sub_clusters.name: Banana Wars and Economic Transformation
sub_clusters.description: The collapse of preferential banana trade agreements in the 1990s devastated Saint Vincent's agricultural economy. The government under James Mitchell and later Ralph Gonsalves pursued economic diversification, with growing tourism especially in the Grenadines (Mustique, Bequia, Canouan) and efforts to develop an international airport.

sub_clusters.name: Grenadines Tourism and Mustique
sub_clusters.description: The Grenadine islands — particularly Mustique (purchased by Colin Tennant in 1958 and made famous by Princess Margaret), Bequia, and Canouan — became elite tourism destinations. The contrast between exclusive Grenadines resorts and mainland Saint Vincent's economic challenges remains a defining feature of the nation.

sub_clusters.name: 2021 La Soufrière Eruption
sub_clusters.description: La Soufrière erupted explosively on April 9, 2021, after months of dome growth, forcing the evacuation of approximately 20,000 people from the northern red zone. Heavy ashfall damaged agriculture, water supplies, and infrastructure. The eruption struck amid the COVID-19 pandemic, compounding humanitarian challenges.
key_events: Approximately 20,000 evacuated from northern Saint Vincent
Argyle International Airport opens 2017 — first international airport
